content:
Owen Phillips: Hey support folks — we’ve had 3 Dedicated tickets this week that are basically “throughput is lower than promised” and we don’t have a consistent playbook yet.

Can someone point me to:
1) the official dashboard we should reference (customer-facing or internal)
2) what we should ask the customer to provide (deployment_id, model, prompt sizes, etc)
3) what wording we should use so we don’t accidentally promise the wrong thing

Also: is “we throttled you” considered an SLO miss or expected behavior?

Zendesk Bot: New ticket created: SUP-4821 (tagged: dedicated, throughput)

Rachel Kim: +1. CS is getting pulled into these and we end up asking for different logs every time. A checklist + canned response would help a lot.

Jasmine Liu: For the last one I handled, the customer was mixing super long prompts + short prompts and comparing to a “tokens/sec” number they heard on a sales call. We need something we can send that explains assumptions / what is measured.

Lauren Bishop: Yep, this is exactly why we kicked off the Dedicated throughput SLO + tier definitions project. We’re close on internal docs but Support needs an interim template.

Question on throttling: the intent is that throttling/backpressure is *expected* when they exceed their tier assumptions (burst ceiling / concurrency), and that is not an SLO breach. But we need to be super explicit about how we message it.

Aisha Bello: Jumping in w/ SLO governance hat.

Current working definition we’ve been aligning on (not fully “published” externally yet):
- We measure throughput as **sustained output tokens/sec** for a deployment over a rolling window (we’ve been using 5m in alerts; 1h in reporting).
- Exclusions: warmup, planned maintenance window, customer-induced 4xx (bad requests), and periods where admission control is actively throttling due to the customer exceeding configured concurrency/burst.

Re: “is throttling an SLO miss?” — No, it’s treated as **expected throttling** (and should show up explicitly as throttled requests / 429s / queueing) vs “we were underperforming while admitting traffic.”

Support should ask for the customer-visible symptoms + a few identifiers so we can line up the right panels.

Rafael Mendes: +1 to Aisha.

From SRE triage perspective, the fastest path is: identify whether it’s (a) customer exceeding tier assumptions, (b) noisy neighbor / misprovisioning, (c) incident / degradation.

If we don’t have the basics, we end up burning time.

Sergio Costa: Dashboards: internal Grafana has a folder “Dedicated / SLOs”. The specific one is:
- “Dedicated Throughput SLO (by deployment)”

Key panels we look at in order:
1) Effective output toks/sec (p50/p95) by deployment_id
2) Throttling rate (429 / admission_control_denied)
3) Queue depth + scheduler wait
4) GPU saturation (SM util / mem / KV cache pressure)
5) Latency split prefill vs decode

If you need a link, it’s: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/dedicated-throughput-slo (internal)

Logan Wright: Metrics naming (if Support is pasting into tickets):
- `rw_dedicated_throughput_output_toks_per_sec` (labels: deployment_id, tier, model, region)
- `rw_dedicated_admission_throttled_requests_total` (same labels + reason)
- `rw_runtime_queue_depth` and `rw_runtime_queue_wait_ms`

If we standardize the intake template, include: deployment_id + region + approximate timeframe + whether streaming enabled.

Kira Thompson: I can draft customer-safe language today for “what throughput guarantee means” + “what we need to investigate.”

We should avoid raw metric names in customer comms, but we *can* ask for:
- deployment name / ID
- model + version (if they pinned)
- example request IDs (2–3)
- typical prompt + max prompt length
- typical output length
- concurrency pattern (steady vs burst)
- whether they see 429s / timeouts

Rachel Kim: + a question: “Did your traffic mix change recently?” We’ve seen customers add a new feature that doubles context length and then call it “throughput regression.”

Jasmine Liu: And “Are you comparing wall-clock throughput during peak hour vs daily average?” A lot of these complaints start with “yesterday 3–4pm was bad.”

Owen Phillips: This is great. Can we turn this into:
- a Support escalation template (fields + what to attach)
- a Zendesk macro / canned response

I want to stop the ad hoc Slack pings.

Lauren Bishop: There’s an engineering support-readiness task already for the template (ENG-2222), but Support shouldn’t wait on that to start using a draft.

Owen — if you start a draft in the meantime, we’ll align it with what Product/SRE are publishing.

Sean Gallagher: For paging hygiene: please don’t page SRE on “throughput lower than expected” without at least:
- deployment_id
- timeframe (UTC)
- whether throttling is present
- whether other deployments in the same region are impacted

If throttling is high, it’s usually “working as designed” (needs tier sizing convo). If throttling is low but toks/sec is low + queueing high, that’s when it can be a real platform issue.

Aisha Bello: Suggest Support decision tree (quick):
1) Customer seeing 429/throttling?
   - Yes → likely exceeds tier assumptions or burst policy. Route to CS/Product for sizing; SRE only if throttling started unexpectedly with no traffic change.
   - No → proceed.
2) Effective toks/sec below baseline AND queue depth increasing?
   - Yes → potential degradation/misprovisioning → page SRE after attaching dashboard screenshots.
   - No → likely workload variability or measurement mismatch.

We’ll have the formal “what counts as an SLO violation vs expected throttling” in the SLO doc, but this works now.

Sergio Costa: If Support wants something copy/paste, I can add a “Support view” link to the dashboard with the right default filters (deployment_id + last 24h). It’s not truly customer-facing, but it helps with consistency.

Logan Wright: Also please capture whether streaming is on. Streaming skews “tokens/sec perceived by customer” (first token latency vs sustained decode). Some customers say “throughput” but mean “time to first token.”

Kira Thompson: Draft response skeleton (customer-safe):

"To investigate throughput, we’ll look at sustained output over a window and compare it to the assumptions for your Dedicated tier (model, context length distribution, and concurrency). To get started, can you share: deployment ID, impacted time range, example request IDs, typical prompt/output lengths, and whether you observed throttling (HTTP 429) or timeouts?"

We should add a line like: "If your traffic exceeds configured concurrency/burst, the system may throttle to protect latency and stability; throttling is expected and indicates you’re hitting configured limits." (wordsmithing welcome)

Rafael Mendes: +1, and for internal escalation add: attach screenshots of panels 1–3 from Sergio’s dashboard. That’s usually enough for SRE to tell if it’s “real.”

Owen Phillips: Action items I’m taking:
- I’ll draft an escalation template today and share in #support for review (fields: deployment_id, region, model, timeframe UTC, streaming y/n, prompt/output lengths, concurrency estimate, sample request IDs, observed 429/timeouts, screenshots of Grafana panels).
- Kira: please send me the finalized customer-safe wording when ready; I’ll turn it into a Zendesk macro.
- Sergio: if you can generate the “Support view” dashboard link w/ default filters, drop it here.

Lauren/Aisha/Rafael: once the formal doc is published, we’ll update the macro to reference the canonical definition.

Lauren Bishop: Works. Tag me on the draft so Product can sanity-check the “what we measure / what we don’t” language.

Sergio Costa: Will do. I’ll post the filtered dashboard link in ~1 hr.

Aisha Bello: I’ll also add a short note on “throttling != SLO miss” to the internal FAQ draft so Support has something official-ish to point to.

Owen Phillips: Perfect. Thanks all — this should reduce a ton of back-and-forth.
